name: Carlos Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in fresh produce and on the tills at a mid-size chain supermarket in the suburbs, and I'm a senior on the team, so I train the new starters. I'm in at six to do the fruit and veg delivery, then I'm on the tills from eleven. I like it when the display looks right and customers say thanks. What wears me out is how the chain's targets change every month, like sell more loyalty cards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that I'll believe it when I see it. At work I'd say it's useful for little things. I'd tell friends not to worry unless their boss starts talking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm not worried, though I keep an eye on things. The self-checkout count in our shop is up to eight, but we still need people on produce and on the door. If it saves me a bit of paperwork, good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and I'd put another 150 a month away. My girlfriend Samira is studying accountancy, so I'd keep the rent low and keep us steady. I'd use the AI tool a bit more, like I do now for writing the produce order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Not thrilled, not scared. A bit of a plateau on my side as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What goes into your money each month, and what pressure does it carry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I take home about 2,300, rent is 800 for the flat with Samira, and I send 100 to my parents. About three months are saved. Samira's course fees are the real pressure, that's 4,000 a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI tools at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then, yes. I ask it to help write the order and the incident notes, and it saves me twenty minutes. I wouldn't call myself a fan, just practical.

I'd tell friends not to worry unless their boss starts talking about it.
think: I'm not **worried**, but I watch the self-checkout count, which is now eight.
Produce and the door still **need people**.
do: Keep going and save another **150 a month**.
Keep the rent low while Samira finishes her **accountancy course**.
Use AI a bit more for the **produce order**.
S0.quote: My girlfriend Samira is studying accountancy, so I'd keep the rent low and keep us steady.
fieldNote: Pressure is **Samira's fees** of about 4,000 a year plus 100 a month sent to his parents.
Practical and balanced about AI: useful, not a fan.
Three months saved keeps him calm but not secure.

steps.text: Keep rent low while Samira finishes her course
Use AI to draft the weekly produce order

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see what the chain does and I'd wait for proof. I'd tell the new starters to learn how the ordering system works, because that's the bit that will change. I wouldn't say much online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ordering, forecasting and loyalty targets will go to software, and so will a chunk of the rota. That's what makes me senior, so I'm half worried. Produce and the floor would still need me, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the chain's free course on the new ordering tool as soon as it's offered. I'd ask the manager to put me on the team that tests the software. I'd put another 100 into savings and keep an eye on assistant manager jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, to be honest. It's the not knowing who gets moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of produce and tills would software change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordering would be the first. The software would see the weather and the sales and order for me. I'd be left checking its numbers and fixing mistakes, which is fine, but it'd be fewer hours of real thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the chain announced cuts to team leads?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what the new job description is and ask for the training in writing. If the team lead role vanished, I'd apply for the assistant manager spot straight away. I'd rather move than wait for the memo.

Produce and the floor still **need me**.

Put another **100** into savings and watch for assistant manager jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need government and employers to sit down now. I'd tell the team to use the next two years to build a second skill. Online I'd share anything useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one is serious. By 2028 the thinking work in the chain's head office is automated, and by 2031 the robots do produce and tills. I'm not sure there's room for a human till lead by then. I'd be 30 and starting again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd lock down costs: cut my parents' money to 60, cancel the gym and try to stretch savings to five months. I'd get a certificate in warehouse automation, which is a short course. I'd ask the manager about moving to the central ordering team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit sharp with people. I'd tell myself to keep calm and make lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is short. What do you do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her straight: we have three months saved, we'd cut hard, and her course comes first, because an accountant is a job that exists in 2030. We'd do it as a plan, not as a panic. She's good at plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you talk to Samira about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Her accountancy is thinking work, which is also exposed by 2028, so we'd both be in the same boat. I'd say we'd both learn how AI tools are used in her field. We'd be a team of two learners.

say: Government and employers need to sit down **now**.
I'd tell the team to use two years to build a **second skill**.
think: By 2028 head office thinking work is automated, and by 2031 **robots** do produce and tills.
do: Cut the money to my parents to **60** and stretch savings to five months.
feel: **Anxious** and sharp with people, so I'd make lists.
S2.quote: I'd get a certificate in warehouse automation, which is a short course.
fieldNote: Responds with **lists and a course** rather than panic.
Notes Samira's accountancy is also thinking work and so also exposed.
Cutting money to parents is the hardest cut for him.

steps.text: Cut the money sent to my parents to 60 a month
Stretch savings from three months to five
Get a short certificate in warehouse automation
Ask to move to the chain's central ordering team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan properly, so let's not waste it. At work I'd suggest a joint training scheme with the union and the chain. Online I'd say little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's better than two years but still not a long time. I'd be 32 in 2031 and the robots in 2034, which is when Samira and I would be buying a place. I'd feel safe enough to plan, but not to relax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the automation certificate in the first year, and put 200 a month into savings. I'd move to the central ordering team if there's a vacancy, since that's closer to the thinking side. I'd keep using the AI tools for ordering, and I'd ask the chain to pay for a supply chain course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steady. I'd say about six out of ten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 32 I'd like to be in supply chain or store operations, not at a till. Running the systems that order for dozens of shops, perhaps. I'd rather be the person checking the computer's work than the one it replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of job do you see yourself in at 32?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd wait a bit on the flat, to see the picture. But I wouldn't put off the engagement; Samira and I have talked about it, and she'd graduate in two years.

say: Five years is enough to **plan properly**.
I'd suggest a joint training scheme between the **union and the chain**.
think: It's better than two years, but I'd be 32 in 2031 and robots arrive around **2034**.
I'd feel safe enough to **plan**, not to relax.
do: Do the **automation certificate** in year one and save 200 a month.
Move to the **central ordering team** if there's a vacancy.
Ask the chain to pay for a **supply chain course**.
feel: **Anxious** but steady, about six out of ten.
S3.quote: I'd rather be the person checking the computer's work than the one it replaced.
fieldNote: Has a clear target: **supply chain** or store operations rather than tills.
Delays the flat but not the engagement.

steps.text: Complete the automation certificate in the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway and we should use it well. I'd tell people to learn something new every year. At work I'd start mentoring the new starters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be calm but not complacent. I'd be 37 in 2036 and the robots around 2039. That's when I'd want to be well out of tills and doing something that needs judgement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study part-time for a supply chain diploma over three years and I'd save 250 a month. Samira and I would marry and buy a small flat. I'd use AI at work to learn how it plans stock, so I'd know the thing I might end up supervising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, quite positive. I'd have a plan and time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a different shape. How would you spend it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the diploma slowly, working through it a module at a time. I'd stay at the chain and ask for a move into operations after two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a good outcome look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A flat of our own, a job in supply chain, and a little saved. And not worrying every time I hear a news item about AI. That would be nice.

say: Ten years is a long **runway**, so we should use it well.
I'd start **mentoring** new starters and tell people to learn something every year.
think: I'd be 37 in 2036, wanting to be out of tills and into work needing **judgement**.
do: Study a **supply chain diploma** part-time over three years.
Save **250 a month** and, with Samira, marry and buy a small flat.
Use AI at work to learn how it **plans stock**.
feel: Fairly **positive**, because I'd have a plan and time.
S4.quote: I'd be calm but not complacent.
fieldNote: With a decade he treats the change as a **career ladder**, not a threat.
Marriage and a flat go ahead alongside the diploma.
Keeps a quiet unease about the 2039 robot date.

steps.text: Study part-time for a supply chain diploma

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because everything arrives while Samira is still studying and we've got three months saved. What would help is paid training while still employed, a clear job ladder in the chain, and a bit of support for the family's money. I'd take that deal.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just this. Most people like me aren't loud about AI, we're quietly working out the sums. If you ask us what we'd do, we have real answers. I'd say that planning in small steps is what most of us do.

headlineQuote: Most people like me aren't loud about AI, we're quietly working out the sums.
portrait: Carlos is a 27-year-old **produce and till lead** at a mid-size suburban chain supermarket, training new starters.
He is pragmatic, tries AI now and then for orders and notes, and prefers proof before he commits.
He has about three months saved, pays 800 rent and sends 100 a month to his parents while Samira studies accountancy.
He answers each scenario with a **course and a move** towards supply chain work.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because everything lands while Samira is still studying.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **training** while employed, a clear job ladder in the chain, and some support for family money.
